The group reported an 81% increase in net profit to $22.7 million in FY2026, compared 
to $12.5 million in FY2025. However, net cash used in operating activities increased to 
$(15.52) million from $(11.37) million. Trade receivables also rose from $75.9 million to 
$117.9 million as at 30 June 2026, with the increase largely attributable to a $41.9 million 
rise in pawnshop loans. 
 
(Adapted from company annual report) 
 
(i) 
What is the current outstanding balance of pawnshop loans, and how much 
further growth can the group accommodate within its existing capital and 
liquidity position? For the non-pawnbroking trade receivable balances, how 
has the ageing profile changed? 
 
Net debt increased by $28.8 million to $94.9 million in FY2026, with net debt to equity rising 
from 46.8% to 58.4%. 
 
 
(Source: company annual report; additional calculation by SIAS) 

(ii) 
What gearing or net debt limits has the board established? Has management 
stress-tested the group's ability to service its debt and meet working capital 
requirements under scenarios involving slower receivables collection, 
lower gold prices, weaker jewellery sales or a contraction in pawnbroking 
activity?

The “allowance for impairment of trade receivables from the group’s wholesale and 
exhibition jewellery business” is a key audit matter1 (KAM) highlighted by the independent 
auditors in their report on the audit of the financial statements. As noted in the KAM, these 
trade receivables are significant to the group, representing 7% of total assets as at year end. 
 
The credit risk exposure on the group’s trade receivables from the group’s jewellery 
business using provision matrix is shown below. 
 
(Source: company annual report) 
 
(i) 
What are the profiles of the customers with overdue trade receivable 
balances? What recovery actions has management taken? Has the board 
assessed whether customer credit assessment, credit limits, payment terms 
or ongoing monitoring could be strengthened? 
 
Separately, the group also wrote off $1.07 million of inventory during FY2026.  
 
(ii) 
What were the main reasons for the $1.07 million inventory write-offs in 
FY2026, and which product categories accounted for the largest amounts? 
What changes has management made to inventory purchasing, ageing 
reviews and stock controls to reduce the risk of further write-offs? 
 
 
1 Key audit matters are those matters that, in the professional judgement of the Independent Auditor, were of 
most significance in the audit of the financial statements of the current period

On 2 October 2026, the company announced the appointment of Novus Corporate 
Finance Pte. Ltd. as its new continuing sponsor, replacing PrimePartners Corporate Finance 
Pte. Ltd., with effect from 4 October 2026. The company attributed the change to 
“commercial reasons”. 
 
(i) 
Could the independent directors explain the specific reasons for changing 
sponsors, beyond the stated “commercial reasons”? Did the board identify 
any new focus areas or new requirements that prompted the change, and 
what improvements does it expect from the new continuing sponsor? 
 
(ii) 
What criteria did the board use to evaluate potential replacement sponsors, 
and what factors distinguished Novus from the alternatives considered? 
 
(iii) 
Does the board intend to pursue a transfer from Catalist to the SGX 
Mainboard? If so, what are the principal eligibility requirements the 
company has yet to meet, and what milestones and timeframe has 
management established to achieve them?
